title: K-injective resolutions compute derived functors
statement: Let $v:\mathcal A\to\mathcal B$ be a left exact additive [def-sp-left-exact-additive] functor between Grothendieck abelian categories [def-sp-grothendieck-abelian] and let $K\in\operatorname{Ch}^+(\mathcal A)$. Then: (1) Any two K-injective resolutions [def-sp-kinjective-bridge] of $K$ are homotopy equivalent under $K$, uniquely up to homotopy; hence $v(I)\cong v(J)$ canonically in the homotopy category, $RvK$ is well defined up to canonical isomorphism, and it is functorial in $K$. (2) A bounded-below complex of injective objects is K-injective. Thus an injective resolution [def-sp-injective-resolutions] $X\to I^\bullet$ is a K-injective resolution of $X[0]$ and $\mathcal H^p(Rv(X[0]))\cong R^pv(X)$ for every $p$. (3) $Rv(K[n])\cong(RvK)[n]$ for every $n\in\mathbf Z$.

proof.text: For a quasi-isomorphism $s:A\to B$ and a K-injective complex $I$, precomposition $s^*:\operatorname{Hom}_{K(\mathcal A)}(B,I)\to\operatorname{Hom}_{K(\mathcal A)}(A,I)$ is bijective by [lem-sp-kinjective-comparison-principle].

Apply the comparison principle to the two resolution maps $f:K\to I$ and $g:K\to J$. It gives maps $u:I\to J$ and $w:J\to I$, unique up to homotopy, with $uf\simeq g$ and $wg\simeq f$. Applying the principle again with target $I$ (respectively $J$) to the two maps from $K$ obtained by composing with $f$ (respectively $g$) shows $wu\simeq\operatorname{id}_I$ and $uw\simeq\operatorname{id}_J$. The additive functor $v$ carries the displayed homotopies to homotopies, so $v(u)$ and $v(w)$ are inverse in the homotopy category and induce the same cohomology maps by [lem-weil-pbc-homotopic-maps-equal-cohomology]. For a morphism of resolved complexes, composing either comparison map with the source and target resolution maps gives the same map from the original complex; the same uniqueness argument therefore makes these isomorphisms commute with that morphism. Thus the identification is canonical and functorial in $K$.

The category $\mathcal A$ is Grothendieck, so it has enough injectives by [lem-sp-grothendieck-enough-injectives]; this is the hypothesis of [lem-weil-pbc-dplus-injective-representative] and of the definition of ^pv$ in [def-sp-left-exact-additive]. By [lem-weil-pbc-dplus-injective-representative], every bounded-below complex of injectives is K-injective. An injective resolution \to I^\bullet$ is bounded below, consists of injectives, and is a quasi-isomorphism by [def-sp-injective-resolutions], hence is a K-injective resolution of [0]$. The definition of $ in [def-sp-kinjective-bridge] gives (X[0])\cong v(I^\bullet)$, and the definition of ^pv(X)$ in [def-sp-left-exact-additive] identifies its hmtBcth cohomology with ^pv(X)$.

The shift of a K-injective complex is K-injective and the shift of a quasi-isomorphism is a quasi-isomorphism by [lem-weil-pbc-kinjective-shift]. Thus $K[n]\to I[n]$ is a K-injective resolution. Since $v$ is additive, it commutes termwise with shifts, so $Rv(K[n])=v(I[n])=v(I)[n]=(RvK)[n]$.

blueprint_notes.text:
**Status.** The source proved the agreement in (2) by saying that a
Cartan--Eilenberg resolution refines both routes, which made this lemma and
the Cartan--Eilenberg theorem [thm-sp-if-e1] depend on each other. Nothing
below uses a Cartan--Eilenberg resolution: (1) and (3) are formal
consequences of K-injectivity, and (2) needs only that an injective
resolution of an object is a bounded-below complex of injectives. The
theorem now cites this lemma and not the other way round.

split_report.blueprint: The steps realize the opening comparison principle and clauses (1), (2), and (3) of the blueprint proof.
